items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.summary:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

items.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
items.summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
items.story_key: model:claude code|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. items.title: CrossEnv: Synthesizing Verifiable Cross-Environment Tasks for Long-Horizon Agent Training
items.summary: Executable synthetic environments provide scalable training tasks and verifiable feedback for long-horizon agents. Existing environment synthesis methods primarily generate tasks within individual environments. However, these tasks do not adequately capture real-world interactions across services, where actions in one service depend on information obtained from another. Synthesizing such tasks is challenging because data generated across environments must remain consistent to support executable and verifiable interactions. To address this challenge, we introduce CrossEnv, a framework that uses an entity-tool graph to identify connections between environments and aligns task-specific data to synthesize executable, verifiable cross-environment tasks. We further propose CrossEnv-Curriculum, which progresses from single-environment tool use to coordination across more environments and business domains, before introducing user interaction. Across four external benchmarks, combining cross-environment training data with this curriculum achieves competitive performance with fewer training examples. Further analyses support the benefits of cross-environment data and curriculum training, and provide evidence of transfer to new environment combinations, external tasks less similar to the training data, and longer workflows.

items.title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway
items.summary: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .

items.title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
items.summary: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.

items.title: Protect sensitive data in your traces: new controls in LangSmith
items.summary: New controls are now in LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data. Learn more.
items.story_key: story|title:protect sensitive data in your traces new controls in langsmith
items.content_excerpt: You can’t run agents in production without governing the data they touch. When that data includes sensitive customer information, controlling access becomes a regulatory and contractual obligation. That puts engineering and security requirements at odds. Engineers need production traces to debug issues and improve agent performance. Security and compliance teams need to enforce least privilege: people should only see the data their job requires. That’s why we’ve added three new controls to LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data: Traces give engineers visibility into how an agent behaved and help them identify what needs to improve. When they record production activity, their inputs and outputs often contain sensitive customer data, such as names, health information, or payment details. Companies need to restrict access to this data to meet: First, they can create custom observability setups with duplicate traces and multiple workspaces. Engineers get trace access, but platform teams have more to configure and maintain. The alternative is to avoid sending traces to observability platforms altogether, preventing agent engineers from having visibility and slowing product velocity. We built these new controls so organizations can meet the needs of their engineering and security teams without the messy workarounds. Here’s how it works. You send your traces to LangSmith with full data fidelity, then grant access to only those who need it. Debugging is handled with least privilege, so addressing performance issues like latency can be managed without exposing any sensitive data. If a customer reports an issue, you can grant access to only that customer’s inputs and outputs, and only to the people or teams required to address it. Everything is configurable through granular admin controls. LangSmith’s new input and output controls give admins greater control over what portions of a trace users can see. Trace inputs and outputs are where sensitive user data most often resides. Other trace data like run trees, performance stats, and metadata are critical for agent improvement and far less sensitive. With these controls, agent engineers can spot and resolve issues – like repetitive or slow tool calls – without seeing sensitive content, and those who need the full picture can be granted access as needed. items.title: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say
items.story_key: story|title:why your fine tuning job takes longer than the flops say
items.content_excerpt: Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs. A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models . The full version will be on arXiv soon. GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move. Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon. We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors. The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs. For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time: Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance. items.title: Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build
items.summary: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.

items.title: What We’ve Learned Building Proactive Agents
items.summary: Proactive agents work toward goals in the background and check in when they need you. What we've learned about memory and UX from building GTM Agent and Robin.
items.story_key: story|title:what we ve learned building proactive agents
items.content_excerpt: Think about how you work with a new hire. In their first week, you give them small, well-scoped tasks, like triaging a bug report or updating a doc. Soon you're giving them bigger tasks, and eventually you're handing them a lofty goal and letting them figure out how to tackle it. They still come to you with clarifying questions or review requests, just less often over time. Agents have gotten good enough that you can onboard them the same way, and like a good new hire, they're turning into proactive problem solvers. Personal agents like Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI's dots popularized proactive agents, which run in the background and work toward larger goals instead of waiting for a prompt. Hone puts it most directly, describing its Engines as AI that is "assigned goals rather than tasks." Goals let these agents take on harder problems that play out over days or weeks. A proactive agent still checks in with you when it's unsure what you want or needs your sign-off before something goes out. When your direct reports get really good at their jobs, you might find that you've become the bottleneck, and the same is true for agents. As they take on more goals, your attention becomes the scarce resource. We think two things are essential to building proactive agents that use it well: memory and UX. A proactive agent responds to events in its environment, which come from three places: The examples throughout come from two proactive agents we run internally at LangChain: These agents operate on all three types of triggers. A few examples: Robin's reviews start from a real-world event, a newly opened pull request, and GTM Agent's daily brief runs on a schedule it created itself after a user requests one. We built both agents on Managed Deep Agents , where more than 70% of runs now come from schedules rather than an ad hoc human prompt. A proactive agent decides for itself when to come to you, and each check-in costs you some attention. It has to be proactive without being annoying . For an executive assistant agent that watches your inbox, that means flagging the message from your boss about tomorrow's launch without also flagging every newsletter. The agent can only tell the two apart if it knows what matters to you, and that knowledge comes from memory . Memory is the information an agent learns over time. The taskforce decided on one central AI Gateway as the shared route for LLM access and governance , establishing a common direction for model access across the company. Building an AI gateway is straightforward, but operating one as an enterprise service is a permanent commitment: provider APIs change, dependencies need patching, security requirements evolve, and users need support. Once applications depend on it, a gateway needs a roadmap, an on-call rotation and a support process. Weighing that against buying yet another AI gateway, five arguments decided why Databricks Unity Gateway was the solution for us. 1. Databricks is integrated with our corporate Microsoft Entra ID tenant, and other AUMOVIO applications authenticate against that same tenant. An application presents its Entra ID token and gets access to Unity Gateway through token exchange, with no separate account, no API key to distribute and no bespoke integration. items.content_excerpt: The current Claude lineup has four generally available models: Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code , you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through. Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level. A higher price per token doesn't always mean a higher cost per task, or a better result. As we showed in Spending your effort , on Anthropic's runs of Terminal-Bench 3.0, the previous Fable, 5.1, at max scored 58.0%, while Opus 5.5 at high scored 58.9% with half the tokens. What's changed

  • Added a confirmation before /install-github-app changes a repository

  • Added a line when a resumed session's earlier messages can't be loaded
  • Added a list in /status of broken agent, skill, command and output style files, keybinding errors, an unavailable sandbox, ignored permission settings and hook matchers that never match

  • Added x-claude-code-managed-settings-checksum to the gateway hint headers; sent where managed settings set CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1, including where they already do
  • Added support for naming a session's billing group with the attributionProject setting, for Claude apps gateways that set admin.billing_group_tag
  • Added /tui classic as the name for the non-fullscreen renderer; /tui default still works
  • Remote Control: Fixed stopping the server in worktree mode deleting a running session's git-ignored files, such as .env
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with --use-anthropic-git-proxy deleting a non-empty directory named by GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL at startup: the runner now keeps it, ignores the variable and warns
  • Fixed claude mcp add and claude mcp remove with project scope deleting other top-level keys from .mcp.json, such as $schema or another tool's servers
  • Fixed /export overwriting an existing file without asking: the dialog now asks, and /export <name> keeps the file and says to run /export
  • Fixed a command you had allowed still running after you pressed Stop, when the approval arrived after a restart, in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions with no feature flags loaded
  • Fixed Enter closing /teleport's load error screen
  • Fixed a click followed by Enter in /plugin installing or disabling a plugin
  • Fixed a half-typed ! command running on an extra Enter after the usage limit menu
  • Fixed some --disallowedTools rules with parentheses in their content
  • Fixed auto mode ignoring some wildcard PowerShell allow rules that name a script with .\, such as PowerShell(.\scripts\build.ps1 *)
  • Fixed a running Code Mode script in auto mode getting permission prompts and denials once Claude started a second script that auto mode also allowed
  • Changed some pre-started background sessions to be discarded after an account change
  • Changed a workflow paused at a usage limit in the terminal to stay paused after a login, until the earlier login returns or you type a prompt
  • Fixed a nested claude with its own token being refused by forceLoginOrgUUID: commands that don't get the session's token no longer get its CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_SCOPES; set it on any that need it
  • Fixed headless sessions losing stored messages on resume when a message was sent again with the same UUID after the process was killed
  • Fixed cases where a session resumed after an empty reply or a killed command lost an answer, or brought back a rewound prompt, after another crash or a move to the background

  • Fixed tasks created after /clear being lost, and cleared tasks coming back, when a cloud or self-hosted runner session with no feature flags loaded resumed later

items.title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.

items.title: H3-Image Day-0 Support: 4K in 0.87s with Vera Rubin
items.summary: H3-Image on Vera Rubin: 0.87-second 4K generation or 6,115 images/hour on four GPUs, with projected API revenue and support across consumer and data-center hardware.
items.story_key: story|variant:image|title:h3 image day 0 support 4k in 0 87s with vera rubin
items.content_excerpt: We brought MiniMax H3-Image to NVIDIA Vera Rubin with vLLM-Omni. On four GPUs, native 4096×4096 generation reaches 0.87 seconds median in our short-prompt serving benchmark. A separate throughput configuration delivers 6,115 images/hour , projecting to 146,755 images/day . At USD 0.06879 per image , using MiniMax's official Standard 4K API pricing example before launch discounts as an assumed sale price, peak throughput projects to USD 105.16/GPU/hour in gross revenue at full billable utilization, or USD 78.87/GPU/hour at 75%. These estimates are before operating costs; the daily capacity is an extrapolation of the measured rate. H3-Image is an open-weight model for text-to-image generation and image editing. One checkpoint handles both tasks in six sampling steps, generates native high-resolution images without an upscaler, and supports up to 16 reference images. We bring H3-Image to consumer and data-center GPUs , spanning NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and Moore Threads (MUSA) , as well as Huawei Ascend NPUs . Oil-paint strokes, a multi-view camera drawing, Japanese poster lettering and tiny words on a rice grain reveal what a smaller image can lose. A game environment adds weathered stone and reflected light. Each uses one H3-Image-generated 4K image, resized to 1K and 2K with its aspect ratio preserved, so composition stays fixed. The two API modes are straightforward: Text-to-Image takes a prompt; Image Edit takes a prompt and one or more reference images. Our main comparisons use 2K (2048×2048) and 4K (4096×4096) output, with one image returned per request. The prompts and reference files stay fixed across machines. See MiniMax's API guide for the request parameters. Choose Text-to-image or Image Edit below. For editing, select 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 reference images ; output sizes reflect the measured cases. For 4K text-to-image , four GB300 GPUs average 1.48 seconds . A 4K image edit with one reference averages 1.77 seconds . A single RTX 5090 with CPU layerwise offload takes 52.29 seconds and 61.45 seconds for those same requests. Each timing includes the complete PNG response. For 2K text-to-image , a single H200 averages 1.49 seconds with BF16 and resident weights. For the detailed coffee-product prompt used here, Rubin averages 1.09 seconds at 4K. The 0.87-second headline comes from a separate short-prompt serving benchmark in Rubin Bringup , not this request.
